newsitem.title: USA: Administration tries to clear up state welfare issue.
newsitem.headline: Administration tries to clear up state welfare issue.

text.p: The Clinton administration said Thursday it would give states flexibility to determine how to spend their own money under a new welfare law, but laid out new guidelines to keep them from circumventing work rules.
The guidelines, to be unveiled Friday, will let states spend their own money to provide benefits to some individuals who lose aid under the federal welfare law, such as legal immigrants.
But the administration is warning the states that if they use their own funds, in effect, to circumvent work provisions in the welfare law they could become ineligible for some federal benefits.
"We are expecting in the near future to give the states some written guidance on this issue," an administration official said.

"The guidance is intended to give the states the flexibility they need to put their welfare to work programmes together, but also make very clear that we expect them to meet the work requirements," the official said.

The welfare law, signed by President Clinton in August, ends a 60-year guarantee of federal aid to poor women and children. Instead, states will receive annual block grants to design and run their own welfare programmes.
In drafting the measure, lawmakers became concerned states might use the new law as an excuse to cut the amount of money they had historically been required to spend on welfare.
So Congress included a so-called maintenance of effort provision requiring states to continue spending 75-80 percent of the amount they spent on welfare programmes in 1994.

In a surprise move, the Clinton administration indicated it might force states to meet federal restrictions in spending their own money. That drew an outrcy from govenors, state legislatures and key Republicans in Congress.
The Clinton administration was concerned states might use their own money to take advantage of the system.

For example, states could set up two separate cash welfare programmes, one funded with federal money and one by states only. The state could avoid federal restrictions in its state programme, but get credit for maintenance of effort rules.
The new administration guidance will warn states that if they are not careful, they might have trouble gaining access to a special contingency fund for unforseen needs.

It also warns states Washington will look at how well they move recipients to work in both state and federal programmes in determining whether they receive special performance bonuses under the law, an administration official said.
